64.etyen:
First attested in 1694.
Borrowed from Latin abrotonum (“southernwood”), from Ancient Greek ἀβρότονον (abrótonon, “tree wormwood; southernwood”).
The ultimate origin of the Ancient Greek plant name is uncertain and it is probably a loanword. Norwegian dictionaries traditionally connect it with ἄβροτος (ábrotos, “immortal”), hence the interpretation “immortal, divine”, but modern Greek etymological scholarship does not regard this derivation as secure.
Compare older Danish Danish abrod (“southernwood”) and Swedish Swedish åbrodd (“southernwood”).

9792.etyen:
Principally from eastern dialectal Norwegian der, dere, object form of de (/di, de/, “you”). This latter is from Middle Norwegian ther, *thi, from Old Norse þér, *þīʀ, þit, themselves from ér, īʀ, it (see these) with initial þ- by rebracketing of the conjugational suffix -ið of preceding verbs. By analogy, the same onset was given to the object form yðr, iðr, yielding *þyðr, *þiðr, whence the before-mentioned der(e), also dør(e). Generalization of the object form of plural pronouns is found in various Norwegian dialects.

Internationalism, based on Latin Belgica and Belgium, from Gallia Belgica (“Belgic Gaul”). Belgica was either formed from belgicus (“Belgic”) or arose as an ellipsis of Gallia Belgica. These names ultimately derive from Belgae, the Roman name for a group of peoples inhabiting northern Gaul.
Forms of the ancient name were used more broadly for the Low Countries before being adopted for the modern state when it became independent in 1830. Roman Gallia Belgica did not correspond precisely to the territory of present-day Belgium.

1004352.etyen:
The modern name is historically the feminine definite form of the earlier stem Mjøs-.
Inherited from Old Norse Mjǫrs f (“Mjøsa”), probably from Proto-Germanic *Mersō f (“Mjøsa”), an s-formation based on the root reflected in merja (“to crush”). According to Harald Bjorvand, the name may refer to the extensive deposits of sand, gravel, and crushed stone around the lake's outlet into the Vorma.

1004864.etyen:
From kongeriket (“the kingdom”), the definite singular of kongerike (“kingdom, realm”), itself formed from konge (“king”) and rike (“realm, kingdom”), followed by Kongo (“Kongo”); literally “the Kingdom of Kongo”. The Norwegian name corresponds to Portuguese Reino do Congo and the Kongo names Wene wa Kongo and Kongo dya Ntotila. For the further origin of Kongo, see that entry.
Parallel formations include Norwegian Nynorsk Kongoriket, Danish Kongeriget Kongo, Swedish Kongoriket, German Königreich Kongo, Dutch Koninkrijk Kongo, Portuguese Reino do Congo and English Kingdom of Kongo.

en.g: A-sharp major; a major key with A-sharp as its tonic
x: The scale is written in A-sharp major.

1005120.etyen:
Compound of Aiss (“A-sharp”) + dur (“major”), literally “A-sharp major”.
The first element Aiss (“A-sharp”) is the capitalized form of aiss, borrowed from German Ais (“A-sharp”). The German form consists of the note name A (“A”) and -is (“sharp-note-forming suffix”); the further origin of the suffix is uncertain. The Norwegian form is synchronically analyzable as a (“A”) + -iss (“sharp-note-forming suffix”).
The second element dur (“major”) is via German Dur (“major”) from Middle High German bēdūre (“B-natural; hard B”), from Medieval Latin b durum (“hard B”). The adjective is from Latin dūrus
